speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening the debate on third reading of the bill to establish a national petroleum company for Canada I do so with a feeling that has degenerated over the months from one of academic argument on the merits or the lack of them in the bill, to one of disgust. While listening to the speeches and reading the debate on this bill I have been impressed with the accuracy of what I said three months ago, that this was a posturing on the part of the government which would not provide any guarantee of more oil or lower prices in the immediate future.
I have concluded that we are just seeing part of a massive fraud on the part of the government to pretend it is doing something to meet the needs of the country. I have taken this view before. When I say "fraud", I am not referring to the type of fraud that is subject to court action such as has now been taken in Saskatchewan in respect of the PFAA. I am thinking more of the political type of fraud. We have in this House at the present time, as part of the whole pattern, a desire on the part of the government to accept a law which would put before the Canadian public debased coinage. This is insulting to Canadians. If there is a desire to raise money for a worthwhile purpose, let us vote it honestly and not try to deceive the people who buy a coin with a face value of $100 into believing they are getting $100 worth of value.
This attitude was also apparent in the budget. There was a suggestion that the government intended to cut back on expenses, and would exercise restraint. As I understand it, the minister asked his colleagues for a cut of $5.4 billion but was able to get an expenditure reduction of only $1 billion. This is not restraint; it is pure public posturing. To me it is nothing but political fraud on the Canadian people.	.
The most massive form of such fraud is contained in this bill. It has been said it will cost from $1,500 million to $2,000 million to set up this company. I think that would be the minimum estimate. Oil companies today must have massive financing; they are dealing with a capital intensive type of enterprise. When we think of gathering the resources of this nation and expending $1 billion or $2 billion just to get started in this poker game, without any guarantee of an extra barrel of oil or one cent less per barrel in the cost structure. I think I am right in saying this bill is a pretence and a fraud.
In my remarks during debate on second reading on March 12 I tried to put before the House, the minister and the government alternative suggestions, which were positive and constructive, as being more useful for the people of Canada than this type of set-up which is merely the setting up of another company. Those better alternatives were in the interests of obtaining access to oil, from any
July 10, 1975

source, faster and cheaper. They were based on the assumption that Canadians as individuals want a chance to share in the wealth of this nation.
I shall again put forward these alternatives in list form, not that they will do any good so far as the minister or the government are concerned but because perhaps anyone reading these remarks will know that there are other and better ways to achieve what the government has in mind as an objective. The first alternative is one which I do not think I would have accepted had I been in the minister's place, but I believe it to be better then the position taken by the government. There are five international companies which control the bulk of the oil industry. Why not buy one of them? This would at least give us the advantage of having in place an organization with 40 or 50 years experience behind it, and it would cost a little less than the amount involved in this proposal. That is one alternative; I do not intend to argue it. It is an alternative which could have been considered and it would have been better than starting from scratch to try to build, in the next 15 or 20 years, the know-how one must have in this complex and risky business.
The second alternative is the one on which I spent the most time on March 12. It is the position of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. The concept is that we have five large, international oil companies doing the bulk of the work in Canada today; and I am not putting down the independents, smaller companies. The position of the Progressive Conservative Party is simple. At present market prices, with the simple provision of an inducement in the budget, in two or three years the Canadian people could own 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the shares of the five main companies, and if there were any profit in this risk venture it would go to the Canadians as individuals who had put their money into it. That was the Conservative position. I think it is in harmony with the philosophy of the Canadian people who want to enjoy the revenue from our bountiful resources. At the same time, it would give us the advantage of the skill and know-how of these companies if we owned them, we would have the advantage of their international connections, and I think we would have a better chance of putting some pressure on these companies in a positive way on behalf of Canada in order to obtain oil faster and cheaper.
On this second alternative I think I am prepared, as a partisan, to travel the country and explain it to the people. I know the Canadian people will respond. Millions of people in the work force, or people who have money to invest in this type of thing would like an opportunity to share, as individuals, in the wealth of this nation. This would allow people who are trying to build up estates to know that their investment would grow with the country and would not be tied to the fixed type of investment.
So I have no apology to make for the Conservative alternative which I think would be much better for the people of Canada. It would be much better in dealing with the immediate challenge of making sure that five years down the road we have enough oil to keep our industrial complex working and enough natural gas to give us a start on a large petrochemical industry of the future.
There are other alternatives, some of which are completely in the hands of the government. A third alternative
Petro-Canada
would be for the government to get off its seat and promulgate the oil and gas regulations dealing with land in the north, without spending a dollar and without waiting another hour. These regulations were put in abeyance in February, 1970, with the result that there have been no regulations available for the companies in the north and offshore since that time. If the regulations were enacted, then these companies, if there is oil there-and there is- could move with the knowledge that the government had laid down the terms in respect of section 58 of the land regulations. The regulations were originally set up in 1961 and they were agreed to by all companies, large and small.
These regulations would give the people of Canada approximately 50 per cent to 60 per cent of the oil and gas found in areas outside the provinces. This, of course, represents the bulk of our oil and gas reserves. The regulations were based on the fact that the government of the day, and all governments, would stay off the backs of the oil companies until there was a tax flow. In return for staying off their backs in respect of all these innumerable government charges, we would expect not 15 per cent of the revenues from the value of that oil and gas but 50 per cent to 60 per cent.
Why does the government not stick with those regulations? The companies agreed to them and I think they would would still go to work on them if the government kept off their backs until they had a cash flow. That is one thing that could have been done. It would at least turn loose these five big companies and the smaller companies who want to develop their properties under federal jurisdiction.
The fourth alternative on which I have spoken many times over the past few years has to do with the question of finance. There is no question now that what has been true for the last five years is no longer true. It once needed $400 of investment to find a field which would produce a barrel of oil per day. It now costs $10,000 dollars, as a minimum, in the north; and if we are dealing with the present method of financing in the tar sands, it costs about $15,000. In other words, it needs an investment of $15,000 to obtain a barrel a day productivity in the tar sands, where a few years ago $400 would have sufficed on the prairies. This new fact of capital-intensive industry means that we have to apply new types of financing. The proposals I made in committee and in the House are acceptable to all the large companies. They will come in immediately under those proposals. The only person who loses under my proposal is the one who collects his money by way of interest. We simply get rid of the debt fast, there is a quick pay-out and then there is more money for the provincial governments, the federal government and the companies.
I have said this before and I will repeat it. It is passing strange to me that the only government in the world which has accepted this concept of financing large, capital-intensive industry is a socialist country, the United Kingdom. Under the system there, a company which has invested $2 billion or $3 billion in a risk enterprise in the North Sea receives an immediate write-off of 175 per cent. This means, in effect, that the government receives little or nothing until the debt is paid, and neither does the

July 10, 1975
Petro-Canada
company. But when it is paid, the people of the United Kingdom share to the extent of 45 per cent to 55 per cent of the gross. This is the type of financing proposal which could be applied not only to new oil and gas areas but also to the capital-intensive mining industry and other capitalintensive industries in the manufacturing sector.
This type of proposal has received great consideration, as I said, from the large oil companies and they are willing to go along with it, but there has been no reaction of a positive nature from this government except that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said that type of technique is not used now. This type of magpie reaction, the thinking that the government only uses ideas which come from its own experts and it will not do anything new, is not the way to build this nation. It is not the way to adapt the new circumstances of high costs, high interest rates and particularly the shortage of capital in a nation which is just starting the development of its resources.
The advantage of this type of financing is that the rate of capital use is speeded up three or four times. If the capital is used three or four times under this quick repayment technique, that is the same as having three or four times the amount of capital. If Canada as a nation were to adopt this technique, we would not only have enough money to finance the hundreds of billions of dollars of capital investment we will have to make in the next 25 years, but we would be able to export capital to other countries which need it even more than we do.
This is the type of thing I would like the Canadian government to do. It is a much better alternative than taxing the people $2 billion to set up a company, collecting a group of green people and some experienced people in the hope that in 15 or 20 years we will have new sources of production. I suggest that a new form of financing should be offered to the industry which would achieve more rapid results at much less cost. The present cost of financing a tar sands operation is about $11 per barrel. If it is done the way I have proposed, using the figures of the oil companies themselves it would be no more than $3 per barrel. This government, the government of Alberta and all the other governments are forcing consumers to pay a cost structure of $11 per barrel, when if it were done properly the cost structure would be $3. That is the significance of my alternative.
Finally, I have a fifth alternative which I think would do more good for the people. It could be done immediately if the Minister of Finance, with the support of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), told the government to end the war on the provinces over the question of taxation of resources. There would again be movement in all the provinces. Nothing is happening in British Columbia because of this war. Where the tax liability of the two levels of government in a confrontation position is greater than 100 per cent, there cannot be investment, and under those circumstances it is no use asking Canadians to invest in resource industries.
Those are five alternatives any one of which would be superior to the fraudulent action we are taking today in pretending that we are doing something. The only argument for this type of thing is that half a dozen countries have similar national companies. There are two American senators proposing one, and other countries are proposing

one to keep up with the Joneses. I might put it in the form of a very simple analogy: if there are five big trout in the stream, all this government will be doing over the next 15 or 20 years is adding another big trout to the stream. Will that add to the wealth of the stream? I do not think so, and I say it is time we began thinking about Canada.
I know that this whole exercise started as a result of a political partisanship quarrel. In 1973 when oil prices began to move up, the minister announced that we should go to world prices. Then he realized that he could have a beautiful fight with the province of Alberta by advocating lower prices. He and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have changed their minds again and now advocate higher prices. This time they are fighting Ontario. Is it not about time we stopped thinking about fighting the provinces for political reasons, and started thinking about Canada?
The alternatives I have listed are sensible and possible but, above all, there is another alternative which I have not mentioned. We have available from our scientists and engineers, for almost peanuts in expenditure, renewable, non-polluting forms of energy as old as the world. New technology could bring these non-polluting, renewable forms of energy on stream in less than a decade, at less cost than applies to oil and gas now.
Those are a few little bits of impetus-just a few things to get us moving in this direction. Last year the government paid a person $54,000 because he had enough brains to put solar heating into his house and it paid off. Consider all the other ideas which come flooding into my office every day. There is a tax law in the United States which in effect prohibits companies from using waste oil. We use oil in our cars and after 2,000 or 3,000 miles we change it. All the technology to clean up that oil and to use it again and again has been there for 40 years. In the United States this amounts to one billion gallons per year, yet we have tax laws which prohibit or limit that type of activity. I simply say, let us have a tax credit for people who re-use oil. Let us give that type of incentive for private industry to start conserving oil.
I could go on, as I have in other speeches, and list any number of alternative proposals. I look upon Petro-Can as a betrayal of Canadian nationalism and as a fraudulent device to try to fool people that they are getting real value for their money. I am a Canadian nationalist, and instead of this concept of putting one more trout in the stream I would like to see much less Canadian money put into owning all the trout in the stream. When we face the country on this issue, I am sure that the vast majority of Canadians will believe the doctrine that they should own their resources, but as individuals and not as the state.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in this final debate on the Petro-Can bill. It certainly has been a long one, with miles and miles of political verbiage, especially from the official opposition, in the House on second reading and in committee where we had close to two dozen meetings. The last remark of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) that the Petro-Canada corporation is a betrayal of Canadian nationalism is one of the silliest
July 10, 1975

things we have heard in this long debate, when we know that the industry is over 90 per cent owned by foreign corporations.
The reason for bringing this bill before parliament is not only to increase proven reserves of hydrocarbons and create more activity in the energy sector of our economy, but to have that done by Canadians. Thinking over the many sessions of the Standing Committee on Natural Resources and Public Works, I am reminded of the old saying "Patience is a virtue". It is almost a necessity in this case in order to maintain one's mental equilibrium. In that connection, I should like to congratulate the minister for his patience because he was able to answer the hundreds of questions during the committee study, many of which were asked half a dozen times.

The fact that he answered those questions so well and handles his portfolio so well is a great tribute to him personally and is also of great advantage to Canada. Members of the official opposition said there was no flexibility in the government with respect to this bill. When looking at the reports of the committee debates, however, we see that many amendments were proposed; some of ours were subsequently withdrawn and some of theirs were accepted. I think this shows a spirit of good parliamentary procedure, recognizing that although the amendments do not change the general thrust of the bill, they further define the capability of the corporation, which of course is what we really want to do.
It is nice to see that we have most of the principal players in the House this afternoon, especially the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies). I do not see the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), however.

speechtext: He is behind the curtains.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Perhaps, with the resignation of the Leader of the Official Opposition, he has already started on his campaign.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that the New Democratic Party recognized the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal Party in announcing the plan to establish a national petroleum corporation on December 6, 1973. They supported the bill on second reading and in committee. The Tories seem to be opposed to it, and that will be defined tonight when there is a vote. We have not had a recorded division except on the two or three amendments at report stage, but they seem to be opposed to it even though it has been before the House for a long time. It was before the Canadian people in the general election of July 8 last year, and it seems that the people indicated loud and clear that they were in favour of it.
It is sometimes difficult to be sure where the official opposition stands on the bill. The group that participated in committee seemed to be a combination of westerners and eastern hardliners like the hon. member for York-Simcoe. The hon. member for Don Valley seemed to be one of the more moderate easterners and even seemed embarrassed at times by the length of the filibuster. I suppose if
Petro-Canada
there is some division within the party on this question it will be nothing compared to the division during the next few months as the leadership campaign heats up.
There seems to be a certain schizophrenia on the part of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition regarding this bill. They seem to be in favour of the federal government investing in Syncrude and the Panarctic exploration. At the hearings they supported the estimates of some $300 million for the Syncrude investment by the federal government, yet they were opposed to establishing a Crown corporation like Petro-Canada to administer this kind of investment.
In the committee hearings they seemed to say, "If you are going to make an investment in oil and gas exploration and development, do it directly." Of course, that would be administered and controlled by the department and the minister responsible. When it came to the Petro-Canada bill, however, they did not want the government to have any responsibility. They wanted the Petro-Canada corporation to be so far removed from the government that it would have no control over it. Their tones seemed to be a diversity of the two opinions as to how this kind of investment should be made by the government. They certainly did not seem to want a Crown corporation to make the kind of investment we have made in Syncrude and Panarctic with the administrative, technical and managerial ability that this corporation will have. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker. Either we establish a Crown corporation with this kind of ability, or we go to the other position of direct investment. The opposition's position on this question seems to be schizophrenic.
The bill makes provision not only for exploration and development in hydrocarbons but for their refining and distribution. The minister made it very clear that for the government to have a string of Petro-Canada gas stations across the country is not a priority and this is not what it wants. However, the development of and exploration for further gas and oil supplies is very important. The opposition spent a great deal of time in committee trying to remove from the bill the powers to refine and distribute petroleum products which at some time in the future may be necessary. Certainly, in a national petroleum company we do not want to remove or restrict such powers.
When we look at the petroleum corporations of the provinces, especially the provinces with Tory governments, Ontario and Alberta, it is rather interesting to note that they have the power to distribute and refine petroleum products. It is also interesting to contemplate what kind of national petroleum corporation the official opposition really wants, when they would require the powers of the corporation to be considerably less than those of provincial Crown corporations dealing with energy.
It seems to me that members of the official opposition see themselves as representatives of Tory provincial governments which they want to keep powers at the provincial level. Or perhaps they are resigned to being perpetually in opposition. I am not privy to their thoughts. Why limit the corporation's present powers? These powers may be necessary in future. If we had limited the corporation's powers, I am not at all confident that we would have been

July 10, 1975
Petro-Canada
able to carry out in future the role that will be required of it.
The opposition is divided in its views about Petro-Canada. Some think its capitalization is too large, others that it is too small. The hon. member for York-Simcoe says it is far too big, that the corporation has massive capitalization; the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Bawden) suggested the corporation is too small, that its capitalization is a drop in the bucket and that it will not be effective. What is the official position of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition? Some opposition members see the corporation as a great plot to nationalize the petroleum industry; others, as a plan for putting many people on the government's payroll. Surely that was the silliest argument we heard in committee.
I suggest that in the petroleum industry, Petro-Can will occupy a position analogous to that of Eldorado in the uranium mining industry. Eldorado is an important producer of uranium, although not one of the giants like Denison or Rio Algom. The larger companies consider Eldorado as an important company but not as a threat. I note that some opposition members suggested Petro-Can would threaten the viability of other, similar companies. Eldorado Nuclear produces significant quantities of uranium and occupies an important position in the uranium producing industry. As I said, we expect Petro-Canada to be to the oil and gas industry what Eldorado nuclear is to the uranium mining industry. Eldorado is going to undertake important exploration work this year. The estimates for that work were before the standing committee earlier this year.
The very existence of Eldorado means that the federal government has available to it expertise in the field of uranium production and can draw on this advice when necessary. In former days of energy surpluses it was not important for a government to have such expertise available to it in the field of uranium or energy generally. But conditions have changed and such expertise is important now. Last fall private companies asked the federal government to participate in the Syncrude project. Such a Crown corporation will employ people who have a grasp of technical matters, and the expertise will be available to the government. So, clearly, one can see the role which Petro-Canada will fulfil, a role in the oil and gas industry similar to that of Eldorado in the uranium mining industry.
The bill stresses the importance of exploration and the development of new reserves. We have developed energy reserves through the use of companies like Panarctic in which the federal government has a 45 per cent equity. That company has developed 13 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in the Arctic Islands. Needless to say, that gas will be important to our future. In addition, the company will be entering into joint ventures with small Canadian corporations which want to explore but do not have the wherewithal. Petro-Can will be involved in these joint ventures. In saying this, I immediately think of Syncrude-type projects in which there was a need for government participation.
A few weeks ago, at the national energy conference, it was announced that in the next ten years we shall need to spend $115 billion, in 1974 dollars, in developing the

energy sector of our economy. I am told that of this $115 billion of capital expenditure, about $49 billion will be for electrical utilities, of which about $20 billion will be for nuclear power and related heavy water plants. The petroleum sector-and this will affect Petro-Canada, although the powers of the corporation embrace more than petroleum matters-will require some $59 billion, of which $21 billion will go to pipelines and about $38 billion to exploration, development, refining and marketing. The exploration and development expenditures will take up an estimated $21 billion, and $8 billion is to be allocated to oil sands projects. It is estimated that development of coal and uranium mines will require about $5 billion and the building of coal gasification plants about $2 billion.
Obviously, we shall need tremendous amounts of capital. We do not want multinational petroleum corporations to put up the money; we want Canadians to be given the chance of participating directly through their government, and we want small Canadian companies to participate in this development through joint ventures. Another important aspect of the corporation will be its involvement in research and development of energy. This is of prime concern to us, and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources will make an announcement soon relating to research and development in the field of energy.
In conclusion, this bill is important as it will allow Canadians, through the establishment of Petro-Can, to make their presence felt in the oil industry. It is equally important to encourage exploration for and development of oil and gas reserves, such as may be found in the High Arctic, offshore and in the tar sands. Important research and development will take place under the aegis of the national petroleum corporation. For these reasons, I am pleased that this bill is to be passed tonight because it will allow us to get on with the job we want it to do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to participate in debate on Bill C-8 to establish a national petroleum corporation to be known as Petro-Canada. The second reading debate was somewhat protracted, mainly because of Conservative opposition. I want to concentrate on those parts of the bill which relate to the entire issue of energy in this country.
The three components of a national energy policy, which we have lacked to date because of the misguided policies of previous Liberal and Conservative governments, are ensuring adequate and reliable supplies, reasonable prices, and that Canadians through their government have a direct share of the wealth of our resources. This government has failed miserably to ensure these fundamental principles of a national energy policy.
The origins of the bill go back to the last minority parliament when the New Democratic Party, holding the balance of power, was able to pressure this government to take some action after so many years of neglect which saw our oil industry gradually being bought up by foreign companies to the point where it is now 90 per cent foreign-owned. Today Canadians are paying dearly for that misguided principle of allowing domination of this vital resource by foreign multinationals. We are paying dearly
July 10, 1975

not only in terms of the price of gas and oil, heating oil and natural gas, but of adequate future supplies.
The very oil companies which wanted to maximize profits by exporting oil, mainly to the United States, argued and convinced this government and its predecessors that we had an overabundance of oil. Export permits were granted to the point where we were exporting half of our daily production to the United States. The National Energy Board finally carried out an independent analysis last year and concluded that we would be running short of oil by 1980. Because these multinational oil companies control 90 per cent of the oil in this country, they are now able to hold Canadian consumers up to ransom by saying that unless they get world prices for Canadian oil they will not explore for new reserves so that Canadians will not run short within five years. That is the kind of lack of policy this government has pursued. That is why we are now in this predicament.
Only two years ago Canadian oil sold for $3.80 a barrel. It is now selling at $8 a barrel and will be going as high as $11 in the near future. The average home owner's heating bill increased by $60 last year and will go up again this year because of the latest price increases. This government is imposing a most regressive and unfair gasoline tax on all consumers of gasoline in order to augment its budget and to make compensation payments to eastern Canadians because they cannot obtain our own oil. By allowing the multinationals to control our oil industry we now have a situation where eastern Canada cannot acquire western Canadian oil. Therefore, eastern Canadians must buy the more expensive oil from the Middle East. This falls right into the hands of the oil companies which, when they were selling oil at $3.80 a barrel, were making a good profit and not complaining.
We have fallen into the trap of letting the companies argue that the price of western Canadian oil must rise to meet the price on the world market. If we had had some foresight and a government that was concerned about preserving control of this vital resource in Canadian hands, we would have had a national petroleum company many years ago. When we reached a crisis stage this government finally awoke to the fact that we need a national petroleum company to regain control of this vital resource so that we will not be held up to ransom by the multinational oil companies. Again, it was only because of the minority government situation that we got the government to move in this direction.
As a country, we have failed miserably because of the policies of this and other governments to acquire a direct share of the wealth of our oil resources. I have gone through this argument on many occasions and will not trot out the statistics again. However, over the years the oil companies have made incredible profits. In addition, they have been able to defer income taxes owing to the federal government to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars. They have been able to obtain depletion allowances and exploration write-offs to the point where instead of paying corporate tax of 46 per cent, many oil companies end up paying income tax of 11 to 17 per cent. Through giving all these concessions to the multinational oil companies they have been able to buy up this vital resource and control its supply and price.
Petro-Canada
Because of the crisis of supply and price the government finally screwed up enough nerve to come up with a national petroleum company which, if you look at the provisions of the bill, has on paper a great deal of scope in terms of power. It can become involved in oil exploration, refining, distributing and marketing. However, whenever the Liberals bring in a bill there is a caveat, especially when it is an idea suggested by the New Democratic Party. It has been traditional for Liberals to accept ideas proposed by my party, using them only in name and not in substance. As an example, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) has just made a statement as to the scope of this national petroleum company. It is very limited indeed.
The national petroleum company is supposed to become involved in exploration. Where is this exploration to take place? Most of the leases are already owned by the multinational oil companies which want no part of this national petroleum company. They see it as a threat to their manipulative powers over this vital resource. In name, this corporation is supposed to do some exploration. In reality, all the best oil leases south of the sixtieth parallel have been bought by the multinational oil companies. There is no hope of the national petroleum company getting involved in this area.
If we turn to the land north of the sixtieth parallel now owned by the federal government in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, we again have a pretty miserable picture in terms of what scope is available for the national petroleum company. I remind hon. members that in 1960 the government set up oil lease regulations for land north of the sixtieth parallel. The regulations were so favourable that within six weeks the exploration permits, which were granted for 12 years, were bought up by the oil companies to cover some 60 million acres, or 93,600 square miles of potential oil producing land in the Northwest Territories. The most likely land in the north that is available for oil is under the control of the multinational companies.
In addition, and this is illustrative of our sell-out principle in the oil industry, the government required that no rent be paid by these companies for permits. All that the companies had to agree to do was spend five cents an acre on exploration in the first year. After the third year, the expenditure had to rise to $2.65 an acre, maximum. The companies that found oil or gas north of the sixtieth parallel were given 21-year leases on half the land covered by their permits. In effect, that meant they could gain three-quarters of the oil under the land that was leased.
The royalty the government would collect from the oil companies was set at an incredibly low figure of 5 per cent for the first three to five years, rising to a maximum of 10 per cent. Foreign oil companies have enjoyed immense profits under this arrangement. By way of comparison, I might say that Alaska, where there are similar geographic and climatic conditions, levies a royalty not of 5 per cent or 10 per cent but of 20 per cent, and in addition the companies are obliged to pay other forms of taxation such as severence tax. Then, again, in Alaska leases are sold at auction to the highest bidders, whereas in Canada they are granted automatically in respect of half the land covered.

It is true the government has gone into partnership with the 19 private companies in Panarctic, but by 1974 Panarctic held no more than 60 million acres and there is no indication from the government that the NPC will buy out Panarctic, making a major move in that direction. Any such ventures are likely to be in co-operation with the smaller, independent companies on the periphery of the oil leased area, those which are not in a position to dispose of land with the best potential for oil and gas production. What I am saying is that the company as presently envisaged amounts to mere tokenism, an attempt to convince the Canadian people, who are rightly worried about the fact that 90 per cent of our oil is foreign-owned, that the government is doing something positive to regain control, ensuring that supplies and prices are guaranteed for the future.
In reality, the company will be so limited as to be ineffective. There is one way to make it effective: it is for the government to use the national petroleum company to take over the largest foreign-owned company in this country, namely, Imperial Oil. This would not only give us access at one stroke to the mechanics of the oil industry, enabling us to see how these companies have manipulated their books at the expense of Canadian taxpayers, but a precedent would be set for other companies in this country. By owning the largest oil company the government would be in a position to set prices.

Mr. Speaker, I think it would be a good point to make, in discussing Bill C-8 and talking about Petro-Can historically, that it was preceded by an attempt to bring in Bill C-32, the petroleum administration act. Going back some years, Canada was doing very well with its oil exploration and energy program and there seemed to be no real urgency for rapid development. We were given to understand, by geologists and economists of the oil companies and by independent geologists, as well as by universities and research organizations, that Canada was sitting on huge oil and gas deposits and had no worries. Most of these deposits were in the province of Alberta; some had been found in Saskatchewan, some gas in British Columbia, also in the Mackenzie Delta and, finally, the Arctic Islands. It was a long history. For many years, in spite of drilling vigorously, oil had not been found in Alberta; in fact, the oil industry there was for years subsidized by eastern Canada. Finally, the wisdom of this course was vindicated when the great Leduc oil field was found and exploited.
After this, however, things went along just the same. We knew we had huge deposits of coal in Alberta, some in British Columbia and a good supply in Nova Scotia: there it even extended out under the ocean floor. We also came to realize that there was a big deposit of oil in the continental shelf, which extends for at least 200 miles seawards from Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. This made Canadians feel rather complacent. However, we were rudely jolted into reality when the oil producing countries and Arab states, now called OPEC, banded together, put an oil embargo on the western industrialized nations and eventually quadrupled the price of oil. This was done only a short time ago.
Since that time the whole picture of the Canadian oil and petroleum scene has changed immensely. There was talk by the opposition for a while that there was no emergency, that the scarcity was contrived by oil companies. But later all the oil producing countries, including Venezuela, Iran and the Arab states, collectively stated their position, which was that oil was entirely too low in price. They said they had to buy expensive, manufactured
July 10, 1975

articles from the west and they were really subsidizing the west by selling their oil at too low a price.
There was some truth in this, but the price rise has contributed further to scarcities and inflation throughout the world. It has caused increasing disparities between the developing countries and the developed countries. It will take considerable time and a great deal of negotiation for the world to try to even up the standard of living in every country, no matter if the Third World countries have energy and mineral resources or not. This is one of the big tasks of the twentieth century, which will occupy us all through the next century as well.
Therefore, today we have a great deal to talk about. We must decide on our oil policy and where, for instance, price fixing, for one thing, should occur. As one views the scene, one thinks first of the oil producing countries themselves. Should they have the whole say in what oil shall cost? We do not believe so. Should the international oil companies operating in Canada have the whole say? Certainly not. The provinces-producing provinces and consuming provinces-will have to co-operate with the federal government to settle the matter. Talks up to the present have not been too successful and they will have to continue. There will have to be an end to confrontation, shadowboxing and just plain political posturing. There must be a definite agreement between Ottawa and the provinces about prices and about how to make sure that the great fossil fuel wealth we possess is properly developed for the welfare of the whole country.
Another question to be settled is whether or not the whole energy picture should be left to the private companies and corporations and whether we should allow the so-called marketplace to determine prices. Secondly, should we press on with our attempt to become self-sufficient in energy at this time? If we were extremely confident about the world's future, and if we could be certain that the other nations who control energy sources would not be selfish about it, then we could really let our fossil reserves stay in the ground for a long time. But we cannot be sure that there will be no future embargoes and we cannot depend on generous treatment of the western industrialized countries by the OPEC countries. For these reasons we must press ahead with development of our energy resources.
Should there be any government interference in the oil industry? Such interference is now pretty well accepted by most countries. The rule of supply and demand in the marketplace is not good enough any longer to ensure a country's future or the world's future. The whole world needs planning, but before that occurs Canada must do her own planning. She must exercise some government intervention in industry and help our manufacturers, our exporters, and assist our small businesses to keep afloat and remain independent. Above all, we must make sure that we are self-sufficient in oil as soon as possible and for as long as possible. To do this we as a government have to adopt the middle ground.
Government interference should not mean government takeover. We do not believe in socialism.

In all seriousness and sincerity, I hope the episode of the final stages of this legislation will not soon be repeated. This is an episode that probably started with the publishing of a document entitled "An Energy Policy for Canada, Phase I" in the summer of 1973-I believe in July-just about two years ago. This document contains a chapter devoted to the question of a national petroleum company, with a reasonable and fair analysis of the arguments for and against. It contains arguments which clearly indicate to any unbiased, rational observer or reader that a national petroleum company is undesirable and is an unwise manner in which to spend the taxpayers' money.
This is a document published by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) just two years ago in which it is stated that a national petroleum company is undesirable. A few months later, on September 6, 1973, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced that the government had decided to establish a national petroleum company. In view of this government publication which suggested this was unnecessary and unwise, why did the government take this new decision? There has not been a single, solitary new piece of evidence given, either then or in the time since, in spite of repeated questions by myself and many other members on this side of the House, to support this new decision by the government.
No new reasons, new data or new rationale have been provided. What an appalling procedure to follow in making decisions involving the expenditure of $1.5 billion originally, now increased to $1.7 billion. The government document to which I have referred suggested this step was unwise, but in spite of that the government has decided to form this company at an expense to the taxpayers of $1.7 billion, without even supplying new evidence, information or data to support the decision. This is a heck of a way to run a country and a heck of a way to make decisions. I am appalled by that sort of decision-making.
It is because of this situation that I hope we never go through this type of episode again with this type of decision-making. No reasons whatever have been provided to counteract the conclusion reached in this document that the establishment of a national petroleum company is unwise. When we ask why the decision was made, we get answers such as the one given to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) during the report stage of this bill. The answer is obvious. Over 90 per cent of the oil industry is owned by foreign multinationals. That is the sort of logic a parent uses with a child to convince the child that he should finish his supper: he is told he should finish his supper because there are people starving in India. That logic works with children but it should not work with members of this House.
The fact that our industry is foreign-owned is a very serious problem. It is about time the government did
July 10, 1975

something in terms of its taxation policies to encourage and permit Canadians to compete in their own industry. If a German drills a well in Alberta, he receives a 200 per cent income tax write-off. If an American drills a well, he receives a 100 per cent tax write-off. But if a Canadian drills a well, he receives a 30 per cent income tax write-off. We cannot compete with foreigners in our own country. Is it any wonder our industry is foreign-owned when that sort of situation exists? Of course not.
We should address ourselves to these problems. We should not say we need a national petroleum company and state participation because our industry is foreign-owned. It is foreign-owned because our government does not allow Canadians an equal opportunity with foreigners to participate in our industry. In spite of the 24 meetings of the committee and the debate in this House, the other aspect of this whole question which is equally appalling to me, if not more appalling, is the precedent it establishes. Up to this point in time every Crown corporation has been formed as the result of a vacuum which the private sector could not fill. That was the basis upon which all previous governments of this country made the decision to establish Crown corporations: there was a need in our society which Canadians as individuals could not meet, and it was therefore necessary for Canadians collectively, through their government, to participate.
This action in establishing a national petroleum corporation sets a totally new precedent in that respect, because there is no defined need which the free sector is unwilling or unable to fulfil. This is superimposed; it represents a whole new precedent which must warm the hearts of the members of the NDP and their philosophical brethren opposite, but it must alarm the majority of Canadians who do not share that philosophy. That type of decision is more in keeping with the traditions of the Middle East sheikdoms than it is of the industrialized world with which we like to think we are associated. I should like to quote from page 185 of the government's document to which I referred earlier, "An Energy Policy for Canada":
Examples of state participation in the petroleum industry are described in Appendix B of this report. Suffice it to say here that it is evident that there is no uniformity of reason and no uniformity of historical experience why these countries, and others, entered into some role for the state in their petroleum industry. The entry into state participation seemed an answer to a particular need within the national community-whether economic, social or political. To a surprising degree, the reasons in most countries were not significantly economic, but related more to factors of direct concern to the state-security of supply, the role of the foreign participant in the domestic economy and its impact on the management and growth of the economy. In some cases the reason was simply the desire to use the petroleum industry as a symbol of what a country could do on its own to increase the pride of its people in national accomplishments.
That is precisely the reason this decision was made. It is totally out of keeping with every decision taken by every government in respect of the formation of Crown corporations. It is that precedent which alarms me. However, in spite of this there is complete lack of a responsible data base on which to make a real decision, and lack of anything approaching evidence for the need for this sort of expenditure with which we are more or less stuck, which I might call a progeny of the Liberal-NDP organic understanding of the last parliament.
Petro-Canada
The minister has the monument he desires for his period as Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The socialists have the toe-hold which must gladden their hearts. The taxpayers of Canada have the responsibility to put up $1.7 billion. There it is. The corporation will exist. We on this side hope it will be a success. We plead with the minister, in setting up the policies under which this company will operate, that no preferred position will be given to this company so that damage will occur to the existing industry which would jeopardize our future security of supply.
We ask him not to rely on Petro-Can alone to provide the Canadian content for further growth in this industry. I ask him to take a look at our existing tax laws so that we might encourage Canadians as individuals to become involved in this industry. I say to the minister he should not think that since he has created Petro-Can the question of Canadian participation is no longer relevant and that government need no longer be concerned about it. I say to him; "Do not give Petro-Can the free money that is provided for in clause 22 of the bill, and make sure that it stands up to the same sort of performance criteria followed by other companies." That will help ensure its success.
I also say to the minister, "For goodness sake do not assume that Petro-Can constitutes an energy policy, because it does not." I have seen references in the press to the assumption that since we now have Petro-Can and a price freeze, therefore we have a national energy policy. That is not a national energy policy. Much more is needed if we are to have the future security of supply we require and if we are to have the security provided by nature of being the only western industrialized nation that has potential self-sufficiency.
So I plead with the government which has this monument not to assume that the energy policies of this country are in good shape and that the problems are over. I plead with the government to make sure that Petro-Can operates properly so that the taxpayers' contribution of $1.7 billion will bring in some revenue in return.

I am particularly pleased to have the opportunity to follow the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). During the course of the few minutes available to me, I hope to bring out some of the points which I think indicate a very real need for the type of action the government is taking by the formation of Petro-Can.
If I understood the hon. member correctly, he indicated that there was no new evidence between 1972 and the time this bill came forward to indicate any new need, and I really wonder whether he has been observing developments on the international scene relating to oil problems as well as our own problems on the national scene. In my view, the establishment of Petro-Canada is probably one of the most significant steps our federal government will have taken in the energy field in the history of Canada since confederation. Over the years we have seen provincial governments across this country, of various political

July 10, 1975
Petro-Canada
persuasions, move directly into that segment of the energy field which deals with the production and distribution of hydro-electric power. We have also seen federal participation in the uranium and nuclear sector and some direct investment in a corporation which has been engaged in the petroleum and natural gas industry. I refer to the 45 per cent federal participation in Panarctic Oil.
The step now being taken by the federal government is most significant in that it will result in direct national involvement, through the formation of a major petroleum company, in the areas of exploration and development of petroleum and natural gas resources. In all likelihood it will also mean future federal government involvement in the acquisition of oil resources where there is a requirement to go outside Canadian borders in order to meet our national needs.
As I mentioned a few moments ago, I would like to draw attention to the need at this time for the federal government to make this kind of move. The official opposition party, both in this House and in committee, has made every possible attempt to downgrade this element of need. We have heard another indication of that from the hon. member for Calgary Centre, who of course was also very vocal on this point in committee. This need forms a cornerstone for the decision of the government to introduce Bill C-8 and proceed with the establishment of Petro-Canada.
The point has been made that private industry has managed in past years to provide Canadians with an adequate supply of oil and natural gas to meet both industrial and residential needs. The point has been made that with some adjustment in the area of taxation, this same private enterprise could be relied upon to meet future needs in much the same way. While it is entirely unlikely that members of the official opposition who have acted as key spokesmen on Bill C-8 will ever permit themselves to be convinced of the sound arguments which have been put forward by the minister and various government members in support of the concept of establishing a national presence in the oil and gas industry at this time, I think it is important that the public understands this need quite clearly.
I would simply like to elaborate on some of the aspects of this argument which have been so ably demonstrated by the minister in the past, with particular reference to the speech he made when introducing Bill C-8 at second reading some four months ago. It seems to me that once this question of need is clearly established in the minds of all Canadians, other detailed aspects of the bill-while most important in the technical and operating sense- become somewhat less critical in terms of the over-all concept.
In passing, I think it is perhaps significant to make some reference at this time to the highly successful Crown corporation which was established in my own province of Ontario in the early part of this century to handle the development and distribution of hydroelectric power in the province. I might add that Ontario had a Conservative government at the time. I am sure the members of the cabinet of that particular Conservative government in Ontario addressed themselves to this question of need and

undoubtedly reached the same conclusions that the government in Ottawa reached in 1975.
This time we are considering the national picture as it applies to future production and development of oil and gas resources, both of which commodities were unknown at the time the Ontario Hydroelectric Power Commission was established. No doubt Sir Adam Beck and other founders of Ontario Hydro looked at the gigantic province of Ontario, reviewed its future potential and decided then and there that the kinds of financing, manpower and other physical resources required a government presence.
Having moved in at the very early stages of the development of hydroelectric power in the province of Ontario, that Conservative regime decided to control the industry in its entirety and no provision was permitted for private sector participation. I think most residents of Ontario would agree that over the years both industrial and residential needs in the area of electricity have been fairly well met by this particular Crown corporation, which has at all times remained a direct instrument of the provincial government of Ontario and has been mothered and nurtured by various Tory governments over the greater part of its life.
I make this reference because it strikes me as rather odd that the official opposition in Ottawa is unprepared to look upon the need for a national presence in an industry as basic to our society as oil and gas exploration and development, when its provincial counterpart in my own province of Ontario has considered such state intervention in an allied field as being so essential as to warrant, not partial control but 100 per cent control to the exclusion of all forms of private enterprise.

The Bank Act provides the only method for the incorporation of a bank, but in my opinion Canadians are handicapped by the structures of the act in putting together a financial system that is not responsive to today's needs. We understand all of the difficulties, and the time taken by the sponsors and organizers of this bank to bring it to this point. But they are far from being in business. We know that during the mid-sixties there were some terrible experiences when sponsors tried to get some bank charters through, but one of them is operating quite successfully now.
It struck me that we are deficient in our total banking system when I saw that a Seattle bank opened a branch in Vancouver this week, calling itself, I believe, Seattle Financial Services Limited. But it is going to offer banking services, Mr. Speaker, and it is exempt from the attentions of the Inspector General of Banks and is beyond the control of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).
One may point to Bill C-7 which will allow incorporation by letters patent. But that does not do a thing, Mr. Speaker. By letters patent they would still come under our present Bank Act, and it is quite incapable of dealing with any but one aspect of banking, our chartered banks. It does that very well, by and large. But the organizers of this bank profess that they want to engage in merchant banking.
There should be a section in the act dealing with merchant banks. And what about the suitcase bankers from all over the place operating in Toronto and Montreal, and these near banks like the one from Seattle? Actually the Federation of Caisses Populaires should be operating
Canadian Commercial and Industrial Bank under the umbrella of a general bank act. These facilities occupy a very substantial part of those organizations providing banking and near-banking services to the Canadian public.
This bank will have its head office in Vancouver but it will operate primarily in Toronto because of the money market. There is a hope for regional emphasis, but I take this with a grain of salt. I remember when the Bank of British Columbia started out it was going to do great things in that province. Almost half of all its branches are now in the province of Alberta, and it is opening more. It is well managed and is doing well but is not a British Columbia regional bank.
These people are going to risk their own money. The inspector general has given his approval, and the committee has reported this bill unanimously. speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Ottawa Centre) (for Mr. Campbell) moved
subtopic: MARRIAGE LAW EXEMPTION-RICHARD FRITZ AND MARIANNE STRASS
speechtext:
that Bill C-1,001, to provide an exception from the general law relating to marriage in the case of Richard Fritz and Marianne Strass, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills and Standing Orders.
He said: Madam Speaker, this is a most unusual bill. Probably this is the first time a bill like this has been presented to the Parliament of Canada. I shall be brief, having explained the matter to some members of the other parties. Very simply, the bill seeks an exception from the general law regarding the degrees of affinity within which two people may marry. The petitioner, Richard Fritz, wishes to marry his half niece, Marianne Strass.
The preamble to the bill, which will be proven in committee, sets out the pertinent facts showing the necessity for bringing the bill before parliament.
Prior to the framing of the British North America Act in 1867, the civil code of the province of Quebec of 1866 was in effect, and it contained the provision saying that a man may not marry his niece.
The next year the British North America Act gave legislative jurisdiction to the Parliament of Canada in the field of marriage and, to the provinces, legislative jurisdiction in the field of solemnization of marriage. However, the degrees of consanguinity are part of the law of marriage, rather than part of the law of solemnization of marriage, and therefore only the Parliament of Canada may properly legislate in this regard. The prohibition against marriage between uncle and niece contained in the code is therefore a matter of federal legislative jurisdiction. Because that prohibition was in the civil code in 1866, section 129 of the British North America Act keeps it in force until it is "repealed, abolished or altered" by the Parliament of Canada.
Since parliament has the power to repeal that aspect of the civil code, it has the power to pass a private bill permitting the petitioners to marry each other, notwithstanding the provisions of the code. I submit, also, that this is the only legislative body in this land which has power to pass this law.
Since the facts relating to the bill are contained in the bill and will need to be aired fully before the committee following second reading, I do not propose to go into any further detail.
I am speaking on this matter having been completely briefed by the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard-Cote Saint-Paul (Mr. Campbell). This man and woman, aged 32 and 25 respectively, have been seeking to marry one another for the past year, but only by presenting a private bill to the House of Commons can they hope to marry. I may say that all these things will be proven in the committee with proper documentation. They have seen their

Also, the couple wish to be married in their church, and the church is prepared to grant any necessary dispensation.
