subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-8, to establish a national petroleum company, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at five o'clock I was at the point of completing my comments relating to the comparison of the origins of Petro-Canada with those of the Ontario Hydro Electric Power Commission much earlier in this century.
We must bear in mind that this particular move by the Tories in Ontario was made at a time when there was little precedent for government participation in the business sector in any form whatsoever. In the case of Petro-Canada the most that the federal government is seeking is participation on a competitive basis with the private sector that, I think we all agree, to date has done a commendable job in the initial period of our oil and gas industry in this country, a period that covers some 30 years since the Leduc discovery.
Let me return to the matter of need as I see it being applied in the case of the establishment of Petro-Canada. First and foremost, and as emphasized by the minister over and over again in the course of our many discussions on Bill C-8, the situation in the area of oil and gas faced by Canada today is quite dissimilar from that as recently as two years ago.
I remind the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), who is not in the chamber at the present time, of the events that transpired during this two year period. First, we experienced the oil embargo that came about without warning and originated with the OPEC countries. We moved from there to the quickly phased-in increase in prices of crude oil imported from these same OPEC countries that resulted in a 400 per cent cost increase for oil imported into that portion of our country that lies in eastern Canada east of the Ottawa Valley line.

July 10, 1975
Petro-Canada Act
An example of this increase in price is clearly seen from the posted price for Saudi Arabian light crude on two different dates only four months apart. On October 1, 1973, this price was posted at $3.01 per barrel, whereas on January 1, 1974, the price had risen to $11.65 per barrel. I should perhaps add in passing that the proposed Conservative income and prices control policy of last year would have had absolutely no effect on this fantastic price increase.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
The third factor that has hit Canadians in a more local or national way is the comparatively recent revelation that recent official estimates of our own Canadian oil resources are now considerably less than those estimates determined as recently as two years ago. For example, the National Energy Board had predicted in 1972, based on its assessment of evidence placed before it, that Canada would have oil supplies available for export, over and above its own needs for all purposes, of some 1.75 million to two million barrels per day as late as 1985. Then, as a result of its 1974 report, just two years later, this same National Energy Board indicated to the government and to Canadians that it will be necessary for us to phase out all exports of oil by the early 1980's. There simply will be no surplus. This has already led to some considerable concern that it may be necessary as early as the mid-1980's for Canada to become a net importer at then current OPEC country prices of as much as one million barrels of oil per day.
To put the contrast in even more striking terms, if we go back to an earlier National Energy Board report of 1969 we find optimism being expressed at that time by this independent body that Canadian oil exports could reach four million barrels per day by 1990. Thus, in a period of five years we have seen our potential national oil production move-in terms of official estimates-from a maximum of up to four million barrels a day available for export 15 years hence, to a new situation which may require net imports of anywhere up to two million barrels per day as of that same date in the future.
I do not think it is really necessary to go any further in demonstrating the dramatic changes which have obviously occurred, and which will be bound to affect the entire oil industry in this country over the next 10 to 15 year period and beyond. The situation is urgent. It is indeed critical.
Coupled with these dramatic developments is the understanding that there will be a requirement for capital investment in Canada in the oil and gas industry over the next decade amounting to some $100 billion. This tremendous investment, together with the vital part that the fossil fuels of oil and natural gas play in both our industrial and residential fabric in Canada, must surely pinpoint the need for much more direct and specific government involvement in just what is going on in this field.
Another factor which comes into play in this overall picture, Mr. Speaker, is a further comparatively recent development in the OPEC countries whereby there is now a clear national government presence in all those dozen or so countries with which Canada becomes involved in

importing oil. For Canada to develop this same kind of national presence may indeed be an important factor in the years ahead as we negotiate for the best deals that can be made in terms of our potentially mounting import requirements.
I think it is also important when considering the need for Petro-Can to bear in mind the attitude of the petroleum industry in Canada toward this new government involvement in a field that, up until this time, has been left entirely in the hands of the private sector. From all I have been able to ascertain, the industry viewpoint is either in favour of the establishment of Petro-Canada or has at least resigned itself to the arguments which have been put forward regarding the obvious need for such a federal presence.
The spokesman for the Canadian Petroleum Association, when appearing before the National Resources Committee in connection with Bill C-8, while not prepared to indicate a firm position on the part of its membership-one which, incidentally, includes the multinational petroleum companies operating in Canada-was in no way prepared to indicate any objection to the concept of the establishment of Petro-Can. It is my understanding that this particular view on the part of CPA has not changed. I think this is important, because it seems to me that the fundamental opposition to the establishment of Petro-Can must now be narrowed down to those members of parliament who form the official opposition. Apparently, unlike their Conservative counterparts in Ontario, they are not prepared to accept the need for government intervention in an industry which is developing an essential energy commodity that is so basically vital to both the industrial and residential needs of all Canadians.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I am confident that the residents of Scarborough West and citizens of Canada generally will in the years ahead look back on this decision by their federal government in Ottawa to create, in the year 1975, a direct and important national presence in the oil and gas industry in Canada as one of the most significant steps undertaken by any Canadian government in recent years.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one thing about which there is no argument is that it has been a long time since the Speech from the Throne. There have been a lot of questions about Petro-Canada, and when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) says there has been a lot of debate and discussion that is certainly a fact. In this debate, we have spoken of the way in which government will now be in the oil game with favoured rules. But Crown corporations are still no guarantee of the objectives set by government. The United States is trying to reach its objectives without establishing Crown corporations.
We can point out that Crown corporations are less efficient and give the example of Air Canada, or that Crown corporations are no guarantee of meeting objectives and point out that the CN had the objective of moving grain in the prairies yet failed in that objective. We could point out that in all likelihood what this particular Crown Corporation will do is to sap staff away from the private sector of society and employ them in the government sector as admitted by the Minister of Energy Mines and Resources.
July 10, 1975

But, Madam Speaker, while we can document that, I would like to take the time I have remaining to answer a rather subtle challenge that wasn't responded to throughout the committee hearings. While I attempted at one time to bring it up, I realized that the committee wasn't the right place. Yet it was very obvious, and if time permits I will give actual quotes from the committee hearings to show that within the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources there was, on the part of those favouring Petro-Can, a rather aggressive and negative attitude toward the producing provinces. They look at those provinces as being non-Canadian. I can quote from committee hearings to show that they took those positions.
I think there was an underlying reason at least for some of us in opposing this bill. There has been a trepidation that has been felt throughout history, that shows why western people have felt that they haven't got a good deal from confederation. I believe, I can establish-I know I can if the time is available-and document, from the time these regions of this country joined in confederation, that they have become looked upon as a colonial state for the purpose of supporting the golden triangle of Ontario.
It is my intent tonight to show that part of the trepidation and fears that are felt in the producing provinces is because all of our past history has not demonstrated that we get good deals from Ottawa. Yes, Alberta does produce 85 per cent of Canada's domestic oil, but the promise of that province lies not in an improved economy derived from oil but rather in the plans for the future that go beyond 1985, because once the oil stops where is the economy?
Agricultural economies throughout the world have always been poor. Check the southern hemisphere and all the developing nations. Agricultural economies are poor economies. Check every industrial nation of the world and where you have within them agricultural regions those are the poor regions. Check Canada. It is the agricultural regions which are poor, unless they have some other resource. That has been the history of the prairies and the maritime provinces of this country.
To some Canadians the west has been a source of agitation recently. It has been recognized. Some have looked and made the comment that Alberta is trying to get out of confederation. Madam Speaker, they saw one issue correctly; there is agitation and there is a feeling of uneasiness. But they read the signs wrongly and gave the wrong interpretation to the facts of the matter. What is really happening is that the west is trying to get into confederation. That is what I hope I can document as I go through this speech tonight.
Central Canada does not know that the west is dissatisfied, and that Petro-Can is but another reason for being frustrated. They treat us like colonial people with our own resources. I would like to give an overview of how the regions of this country have been treated by the federal government. For over 100 years central Canada has had protection of tariffs. The colonial regions paid more money than central Canada did for textiles, for automobiles for farm machinery, for manufactured products. All of those products were obtainable cheaper from the United States and Europe, and from Southeast Asia. But the regions of the country paid dearly for them.
Petro-Canada Act
But the regions of the country paid clearly for them.
Many members of the NDP and the Liberal party are condemning the oil companies. They paint them as devils opposing Canadian society. I ask, Madam Speaker, where was the federal government 30 years ago when the producing provinces were begging for help, looking for someone to try to help them develop the industry?

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
I notice that the chickadees opposite have been into the fermented choke cherries again. How does this country justify Ottawa's refusal to listen to Alberta in 1959, again in 1967, and then in 1970 when the province wanted to extend the pipeline to Montreal? To extend that pipeline would have added one or two cents per gallon to the price of gasoline east of the Ottawa valley. But oh no, east of the Ottawa valley they could get oil cheaper from Venezuela, and if it could be had cheaper there was no sense, in their opinion, in buying oil from one of the regions.
What happened then, Madam Speaker? All of a sudden Alberta's oil is worth $11 a barrel on the world market. At last there is a chance to make a dollar. What does Ottawa do but insist that Alberta's oil go to the rest of Canada at $6.50 a barrel? After all, they say, it would be good for the whole of the country. Is "central Canada", Canada as a whole? Everywhere east of the Ottawa valley energy is imported mainly from Venezuela at the world price. To cushion that blow, Ottawa tacks an export tax of $5.50 a barrel on Alberta oil headed for the United States, using that tax to help pay Venezuela. This means that the price of oil east of Ottawa is at least close to the price in the rest of central Canada. But it also means that Alberta cannot even make a dollar on the 900,000 barrels a day going south.
That is very nice for central Canada, but the producers see it as pick-pocketing. If we are truly a confederation, then it must be a confederation both ways. If we are going to have cheaper oil across the country, then we must talk about other products as well being cheaper across the country. The "good of Canada" is being interpreted by the federal government as the "good of central Canada"; it is not talking about a whole nation from sea to sea.
If this government really feels it is being responsive to the regions, then we can ask some legitimate questions. Let me ask the members on the other side how it was they accepted the fact that the great depression lasted a full three years longer on the Prairies than in this part of Canada. I see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is rather excited at the moment. Let me ask hon. members opposite to justify why it is that western Canada pays twice as much to bring manufactured rapeseed back from Toronto to Lethbridge than it does to ship raw rapeseed per ton from Lethbridge to Toronto. Or why is it that iron and steel products from Toronto are cheaper when shipped to Vancouver than when shipped to Saskatoon? Or why are manufactured goods cheaper when shipped to Vancouver and back to Calgary than when they are shipped directly to Calgary? If we are going to talk about cheap oil

July 10, 1975
Petro-Canada Act
for all of Canada, those are the kinds of questions that must be answered.
As another example, it costs $1.50 per hundredweight to ship lumber from British Columbia to Calgary, whereas it costs only $1.79 per hundredweight to ship that same lumber from Terrace, B.C. to Toronto. All of these are matters that must be answered before we can talk about one product being cheaper for this part of the country. Even today there is no ongoing policy to assure the colonial regions a fair economy or a just place in confederation. The prairie regions that are agricultural are treated only with crisis kinds of policies. The recent LIFT program was legislation that came at the moment of crisis. The fact of the matter is that it was like a box of band-aids being sent to the scene of an aircraft crash; it did not do anything for the agricultural concerns of the regions. What it did was to destroy absolutely many of the markets that were already there.
In my area the farmers sing on Saturday nights "Where have all the flour mills gone?" We know where they have gone, Madam Speaker. They have gone, because of prejudiced freight rates, to central Canada. They do not associate themselves with where the product is produced.
Let me give another example. It is cheaper to ship live western cattle to Ontario and feed them with grain grown in the west and shipped to the east under subsidy at low rates, than to slaughter the cattle in the west and send them east for consumption. That, Madam Speaker, documents another case where an industry has been taken away. But according to the federal government it is the business of the west to supply the resources for central Canada, and then in turn to be a market for central Canadian industries.
To keep this in perspective, I think it is important to note that as recently as 1965 the province of Alberta was still receiving equalization payments. We were basically a single industry province-an agro-economy. Then came oil and a chance to get into confederation. Now we have Petro-Can, because someone says it is for the good of central Canada.
While we are talking about what is good for Canada, let me ask this. Why cannot the Wheat Board have its headquarters in western Canada? What cannot the salt fish committee operate in the maritimes? Why cannot the National Energy Board be based in Calgary, since every time they have a meeting that is where 80 per cent of the delegates come from?
As I say, Alberta was an agro-economy before it had oil, but now oil has become our bread and butter. Oil to the western provinces is the same as the auto industry, the textile industry, the mining industry and manufacturing for Ontario. Oil, Madam Speaker, became our hope.
I think the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) gave an excellent speech on January 1 of this year. What he talked about was sharing. This is important in confederation, in this land from sea to sea, but though the concept is good I think the Prime Minister failed to go far enough. The Prime Minister stated:
I invite my fellow citizens to rejoice in what has been given to us as Canadians-the good fortune to be united in a federation, a system of government whose most distinct attribute is the sharing of wealth.

The sharing of wealth is not the full concept of sharing. What the producing provinces are asking the other provinces is not just to share our wealth and other things. What we want is a share in participation. What we want is to share ideas. What we want is a share in planning the development of this country. Petro-Canada is an imposition on the part of central government. The fact of the matter is that this government does not trust the producing regions to take care of Canada as a whole, and that is a challenge that I think the government has to answer. Why the distrust?
It is well known that the British North America Act gave to the provinces the right to their resources. There is also no doubt that this whole program is one of distrust. The real question is one of trust. Let me point out for the consideration of the House that disparities still exist. I ask those government members who are so excited about Petro-Canada to justify why it is that central Canada still gets $55.9 million from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion while the western provinces only get $4.2 million, which works out on a per capita basis to $4.05 per head in central Canada but only $1.07 in the prairies.
As far as the banking industry is concerned, Madam Speaker, it is to be noted that virtually every head office in Canada is located in either Toronto or Montreal.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this bill to establish a national petroleum company merits our support for, among others, two very important reasons. First, Petro-Canada will increase the opportunities for industrial research and development in the crucial area of energy resource production. As I have shown in this House on several occasions, our industrial research and development effort in Canada is inadequate and appears very small, indeed, when compared with the activities in this area of other technologically advanced OECD countries.
As a Canadian company without multinational ties, Petro-Canada will require the establishment of an exten-

July 10, 1975
Petro-Canada Act
sive, independent research and development facility. I would stress the word "independent" as this is the first opportunity we have had to set up a facility of this nature and magnitude, free from the whims and priorities of foreign head offices. I cannot emphasize too greatly the importance of industrial research and development in the over-all energy picture and for our economy as a whole.
This activity furnishes the building blocks which enable us to follow the innovative process from the genesis of a new idea right through to the successful marketing of the resulting technology and product. That is a second reason for this bill's importance. New opportunities will open up through this measure for Canadians to gain practical experience in the international oil business at the very highest level. The resultant co-ordination of activities will lead to greater economies of production and increased opportunities for leadership in the industry.
As the 1974-75 annual report of the Science Council of Canada points out, Canada has been content to rely on our corporate relationships, which means primarily the Canadian subsidiary of a foreign parent company, to link us to technological developments being promoted outside the country. The report points out that this lack of economic, and therefore technological, sovereignty has meant that decisions regarding the pace and manner of development of some of our natural resources are made outside Canada. Petro-Canada will be in a position to help rectify this situation.
One of Petro-Canada's major objectives will be to assure an adequate supply of energy for Canadian needs. As the Syncrude project has shown, this task can be, and usually is, both risky and expensive. We are no longer in a position that would allow us to leave the question of continuation of supply in the hands of those whose motivation in this regard is only profits. To ensure the maintenance of public confidence in itself, Petro-Canada will necessarily have to be run as a profitable concern. However, the public will at least have the knowledge that, should times become hard for the oil companies, Petro-Canada will not pull up stakes and move out of the country. The company's participation in Syncrude will allow it to monitor that operation and ensure that all partners are working in the best interests of the Canadian people.
It is imperative that the government have a strong say in the development of energy resources in this country, as the possible consequences of ignoring that responsibility could critically alter our way of life which is so dependent on a constant supply of energy.
We must also bear in mind that Petro-Canada's mandate gives it authority to develop forms of energy other than petroleum. Our energy requirements are supplied by a "product mix" of energy forms. For example, electricity is generated through the use of several of these-hydro, nuclear power, coal, oil and natural gas. As the relative use of these energy forms changes, that "product mix" alters to reflect the economics involved in the use of each form. Only one organization is concerned with the development of all these energy sources, and that is the federal government. Petro-Canada will provide the government with the commercial arm which will enable it to implement

changes in the relative use of these resources. Petro-Canada is therefore extremely adaptable to change, and this capability gives it a great advantage in working to fulfil its purpose of ensuring a continuous supply of energy for Canadians.
Petro-Canada will enable Canadians to become world leaders in the development of new technologies designed to solve the problems inherent in oil exploration in the far north. These difficulties are compounded when Arctic drilling is done off-shore, involving the establishment of facilities on ice and water. A well planned research and development effort is required to overcome these difficulties. Once the expertise is developed, however, Petro-Canada will be in a position to engage in the exploitation of deposits in technologically hostile regions around the globe.
As exploitation of reserves becomes less economical, new technologies must be developed to increase the total ultimate recovery of oil and gas in marginal fields. Research and development will be confined not only to the extractive and refinement processes, but also to problems of logistics, transportation, and environmental protection. The challenge is great, and the timing of this bill is extremely appropriate. The opportunities for significant achievements by Petro-Canada in the field of energy development are very great.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think at this stage of the debate on Petro-Can it would be desirable to look at the philosophy of this bill which places the Government of Canada squarely in the middle of one of the most capital intensive and one of the most risky businesses known to man. The principal question then is whether the Government of Canada should be in the oil and gas business and, if so, why.
The minister who appears still to be a babe in the woods, or at least sleepwalking as it relates to the realities of the oil and gas business, has blundered ahead, followed by his equally misguided colleagues, to ram and drag this ill-conceived piece of legislation through the House and the committee to its present advanced stage. A number of important points and facts are now on the record regarding Petro-Can's future, and in addition several important and appropriate amendments were made by this party.
I maintain in the strongest terms, however, that the minister and his minions have not convinced opposition members of the committee or of the House that at this critical time in the economy of Canada, or for that matter at any time in the future of this country, a national petroleum company is required or desired by the citizens of Canada.
Why should the Canadian taxpayer be financing, at huge cost and at high risk, a national oil company? The minister's answer to this question can be found by looking at the objectives of the company as stated by the minister in the House, and by his parliamentary secretary as well. The minister and the parliamentary secretary said over and over again, through their speeches in the House and their answers in the committee, that the principal objective and the prime need to be filled by this Crown corporation, Petro-Can, is that of making available to Canadians adequate supplies of oil and gas at reasonable prices. The
July 10, 1975

minister said that compelling reasons for creation of a national oil company relate primarily to security of supply from our domestic resources and also possibly from abroad. This seems to be the principal argument put forward by the government to attempt to justify this lame bill, and in the months ahead this lame company, to the people of Canada.
I think anyone with funds such as will be in the hands of Petro-Can could buy production, thus creating nothing in the way of reserves, and by merely taking over an existing oil company can buy into the oil and gas business and probably fairly quickly show a profit, but that has nothing to do with the creation of new reserves of oil and gas at a reasonable price, or additional supplies for Canadians.
I do not think that any knowledgeable individual in the oil industry would deny that an expenditure of $1.5 billion over a period of time will find reserves of oil and gas, although I think most Canadians who look at the operation and performance of Crown corporations already in existence will agree that generally their ability to serve the needs of the country and to reduce costs falls a long way short of the example provided by the private sector. Surely the best example of this took place during the oil crisis in late 1973 and early 1974 when the Department of Supply and Services under the direction of its minister made, according at least to the words of the parliamentary secretary, one of the best deals for the purchase of oil at something in the order of $1 a gallon, at which point in time oil in the rest of the world was sold at a fraction of that price. This is an example of the type of problem the government gets into when it attempts to compete in the world and with the private sector. I believe that the government and the minister are deliberately or through ignorance misleading the Canadian people in trying to sell this bill on the grounds that it is the solution to this vital and critical problem of supply.
It is interesting that, when questioned in committee, the minister was unable to give any figures whatsoever on what oil or gas Petro-Can might produce at any time during its expenditure of the first $1.7 billion. All the minister could say was that the company would be subject to the disciplines of the balance sheet and a profit and loss statement. He did not say whether such discipline would require that the company show any profit, or whether in fact the balance sheet would show any assets after the $1.7 billion had been expended by way of exploration and drilling of holes in the ground.
Just this week one further horrible example was brought to light with regard to how Crown corporations subject themselves, as the minister says, to financial disciplines. An inquiry into the operations of Air Canada was told that the Crown company had a Mickey Mouse accounting system. That may be because Canada has a Mickey Mouse government. Air Canada deliberately concealed information and tampered with its accounts to hide the facts from a committee of this House. I think that is shameful. All of this was done to cover up well over $1 million which was lost by the company through one of its subsidiaries.
Petro-Canada Act
With the powers and the flexibilities granted to Petro-Canada in this bill, the areas open to abuse, bungling and failure could make the performance of Air Canada, the Post Office, and all Crown corporations put together since confederation look like a mild error by comparison.
The fiasco at Air Canada today is perhaps just the tip of the iceberg, but let us compare in size Air Canada to this new creature, Petro-Can. Petro-Can is to have an initial capital of $500 million, more than ten times that of Air Canada. Adding its proposed borrowing of in excess of $1 billion will give Petro-Canada total funds of something more than 150 per cent of those available to Air Canada.
This new Crown corporation, like some Crown corporations, is to be immune from the audit and normal checks by the Auditor General of Canada. Just today the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) refused the request of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) to permit the Auditor General to audit Air Canada's accounts. Petro-Can will be by far the most powerful of all Canadian government enterprises. It will be a monster in disguise, sold to the Canadian people as the solution to Canada's energy shortage problems.
The Auditor General reports to parliament. More is required in the Petro-Can audit than just an opinion on the financial statements. Based on the conclusions of the independent review committee which was set up and which reported on the office of the Auditor General recently, this Crown corporation should be audited or co-audited by the Auditor General. Perhaps the minister in the course of speaking tonight will say something about this important fact and perhaps confirm to the House that the Auditor General will at least be a co-auditor of Petro-Can. If the minister does not, it would seem to me that this would clearly be an indication of the intention of the government not to make the facts of this corporate operation available to this House.
In view of the exposure which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has had and the advice he has had from the private sector, he must now be considered as one with a significant degree of information, and one must ask why this government is moving into the oil and gas business at this time. The first mention of such a step was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the fall of 1973 when bowing, as the government continually did, to the demands of the New Democratic Party. The government agreed to create a national oil company.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased tonight, July 10, to speak on a subject which I first spoke upon on December 7, 1973, some two and a half years ago. It has taken that long to get this bill to where it is. There has been a tremendous amount of opposition, and I am very pleased we are at this point that the bill will be passed before the end of this sitting.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced on December 6, 1973, that we intended to go ahead with Petro-Can-some called it "Oil-Can"-there were discussions about our federal energy policy. In a speech I gave on December 7 I indicated three major areas of this energy policy in which Petro-Can would fit extremely well, and I should like to go over them again tonight. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) mentioned them and took them as his own, but I would recall to hon. members that I enumerated them on December 7, 1973.
The first ingredient of a Canadian energy policy is a secure supply, which means making Canada self-sufficient. This became a real problem because in 1972 we were told that 130 billion barrels of crude oil were ultimately recoverable. Today we are talking about 50 billion or 60 billion barrels, and in the meantime we have taken out perhaps four or five billion barrels.
The second part of a policy that we enunciated was the single reasonable price across Canada. We set a price of $6.50 per barrel, which goes now to $8. That is still $4 below world prices. I challenged hon. members opposite in committee a year ago when I said, "I think you would like $8 per barrel," and they did not say they objected to it at all. I am saying now that we have maintained a single fair price, and $8 per barrel is the new price, $4 below the world price.
The third ingredient in a Canadian national energy policy is more Canadian control and Canadian ownership.
I should like to look at Petro-Can very briefly now as I know one or two other members wish to speak before the debate winds up. I should like to look at Petro-Can as it relates to these major purposes, the first being self sufficiency in supply. The second thing is to show that we do have single fair price. In this case we are talking about a Canadian nationally owned company that will monitor this industry. The third purpose is to increase Canadian ownership and Canadian control of the industry. I should like to deal with these three purposes very briefly.
In committee members of the Conservative party kept talking about what a fine industry the oil industry was, and how straightforward and so on they were. But the information that was being supplied to the National Energy Board was coming from the industry. It was coming from other sources too. When we went into 1972 we were told, and when we came here and sat in 1973 committees we were told that there were unlimited quantities of oil-that we were talking about 130 billion barrels. We were told by hon. members opposite that we should not be limiting our exports to the United States when we decided to put a quota on in the spring of 1973. We were told these things, but this is the industry that now has to admit there is a shortage-this is the industry that is concerned about a shortage just three short years later. Do not forget that.

Madam Speaker, we were informed in the spring of 1973, although the 130 billion figure was arrived at in 1972.
It is absolutely imperative for us to increase supply, and it is important to set up a Canadian-owned company which will do this. Not only do we need to find more oil; we must conserve it.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext: Then why not introduce a proper tax policy?

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
I know some members are angry about the establishment of Petro-Can, but even they must admit that its involvement in Syncrude will be useful. Initially, I understand the company will spend about $300 million in that area.
You know, there is always the danger that multinational companies will find oil supplies elsewhere and move. Therefore we need a Canadian-based and owned company which will explore exclusively in Canada, and in the north, and support Syncrude-type projects.
Second, by setting up Petro-Can we can monitor the industry. People do not trust the petroleum industry. I think you will find there is general distrust. The petroleum industry made huge mistakes which eventually influenced what are now the OPEC countries to form a cartel and just about quadruple oil prices around the world.
This morning's Globe and Mail carried a full-page advertisement which reads:
Here's where your money goes for those gasoline price increases-
Federal excise tax of 10 cents a gallon, effective June 24, 1975, 100 per cent to the federal government.
That is all it says. The advertisement does not say that the money will be used to equalize the price of oil across the country. The advertisement also says that the coming increase of $1.50 a barrel in crude oil prices will go entirely to the federal and provincial governments. Nothing is said about moneys being returned to the companies if they explore. The industry does not tell you these things.
The industry has been investigated by the U.S. Congress; it has been investigated elsewhere in the world. The huge fluctuations in oil prices which took place during the 1973 energy crisis are also being investigated.
I submit that we shall only know the workings of the petroleum industry in this country if the government sets up a national company and, through it, monitors the workings of the entire industry.
My third point is that the establishment of this company will enable us to retain some degree of Canadian control. The development phase of the industry is 90 per cent foreign-owned, and the refining phase 99 per cent foreign-owned. The five largest oil companies in Canada, Imperial
[Mr. McRae.)
Oil, Gulf, Shell, BP and Texaco control $6.6 billion worth of assets. The members of the Conservative opposition were not concerned about this degree of ownership when we discussed the bill in committee, yet they are members of the party which said one and a half years ago during a convention that within ten or 15 years they want to see this country own 75 per cent of this industry.
Day in and day out they have objected to the size of Petro-Can. "Keep it small" is what they said. If Petro-Can reduces foreign ownership even by 25 per cent or less, its establishment will have been worth while. Frankly, I do not think this operation is too big for Canada, although Conservative members seem to think it is.
Conservative members oppose the Canadian people owning a company which will compete with multinational companies. They see no advantage in such a company. They demanded that a company owned by the people of Canada should have no preference over a multi-national. I find their position hard to understand. One hon. member actually spoke about Petro-Can being imposed upon the people of Alberta. He did not talk about companies whose offices are outside Canada, in Texas, Alabama, Georgia, Britain, or Holland imposing their wills on the people of Alberta.
Alberta will gain greatly from the establishment of this company. The province will be the gainer if Syncrude-type projects are developed. The province of Ontario will gain; all Canada will gain from the setting up of this company.
In conclusion, let me say that in 1973 we announced our policy, and Petro-Can will help us to carry it out. It will help to obtain secure oil supplies for the people of Canada and help us to monitor the industry so that we can be sure of a fair price. Further, it will decrease foreign-ownership in the industry, perhaps to 75 per cent.

Madam Speaker, as I rise in the final minutes of this debate, having made a contribution on second reading four months ago and realizing that many words have been spoken since then on this topic, I am reminded of something which happened in the British House. A member asked for guidance of the Chair on the length of speeches. The Speaker replied something like this, "My guidance is this: I hope all speeches will be as short as they can be." My speech will therefore be only half as long as it would otherwise have been.
Over the week end I heard a CBC news announcer say that the recent federal budget had been easily passed. I suppose that tonight we shall hear him say that Bill C-8 passed easily. A majority government of course can pass any bill it wishes easily, but that does not mean that opposition members should not vigorously oppose legislation which they believe to be not in the best interests of Canadians.
Bill C-8 was introduced on October 3, 1974, nine months ago. Since then what has happened to the petroleum industry? I am sure I speak conservatively when I say that oil exploration has been greatly curtailed. This means that our drilling rigs have moved to other countries. Federal and provincial governments have been squabbling, acting unilaterally, and aggravating an already difficult relationship.
July 10, 1975

The oil industry sounded the alarm. The Canadian Petroleum Association has sounded the warning in a small brochure which it puts out, saying that we can choose between one of two alternatives. It explains what will happen if no exploration takes place. Canada will be short of oil. It states that if Canada explores and develops, there will be oil. Of course finding, developing, transporting, refining and marketing are a costly business. They estimate the cost at $30 billion.
There has been a lot of criticism about oil company profits. In the industry's brochure it is pointed out that the profits for the years 1970 to 1973 were about 12 per cent. That is not much more than the yield on the government's Canada Savings Bonds which bear no risk.
The government has indicated that it wants to cut expenditures. Here is the oil industry offering to save it a $30 billion expenditure to find oil. Recent remarks by other industrialists in this country have indicated the dissatisfaction and lack of wisdom in the course the government intends to follow.
At the annual meeting, Ian Sinclair of Canadian Pacific, a group of companies, talked about examples of government involving itself unnecessarily in business functions. He said:
Such intrusions are frequently accompanied by the explanation that "business has failed" to do this, or to do that. What has usually happened is that business has been prevented from doing it because of tax policies, or government interference with markets, or uncertainties injected either by sudden changes in government policies or by contradictory policies at different levels of government.
He went on to say that Canadians have felt that our abundant natural resources were our surest guarantee of future wealth, but now federal and provincial governments are squabbling over them like contending heirs. He also commented on the risks involved in searching for resources. He said:
There is enough risk in resources development without injecting these additional hazards.
The risks that are inherent in resource projects cannot be reduced by transferring them to public ownership. That would simply enforce risk-taking on a lot of people who do not want it. Moreover, results of publicly owned enterprises both here and abroad give us fair warning of the disappointments that public ownership breeds.
There are other statements which, in the interest of time, I will skip.
In my remarks in the second reading debate, I drew attention to the abysmal performance of the government in operating its 59 Crown corporations that now exist. This month on the desk of all hon. members appeared the Labour Canada information sheet. In summary, it states that in April of 1975 there were ten work stoppages in the federal jurisdiction that involved 6,007 workers and the loss of 126,000 man-days. Such a lack of management skills is bad enough in the post office, airlines and so on, but what if it were in the national petroleum company? It would be far more serious.
The fundamental principles should be that the government takes a low profile and provides those services that are necessary and that the enterpriser cannot or will not provide. However, this government wants to involve everybody in a direct manner. It refuses to recognize that
Petro-Canada Act
the corporate giants are really just a legal piece of paper. They are all made up of shareholders who are eventually just people. For example, every worker in Canada who contributes to a pension plan has an investment in some corporate giant.
One might pause to give serious thought to the effect on the enterprisers of Canada, and the enterprise system which has built Canada, of government action such as Bill C-8. That well-known enterpriser from Toronto, John Bulloch, tailor, recently placed an advertisement which related to the old story of "The Little Red Hen" in political terms. After the cries of "excess profits", "capitalist leech", "equal rights" and so on, the little red hen was forced to give up 80 per cent of the production of bread for the benefit of her barnyard neighbours. Predictably, of course, the neighbours always wondered why the little red hen never baked any more bread. One might ask when Canadians will wake up one morning and wonder why the oil industry has not produced any more oil for their factories, furnaces and automobiles.
Finally, I would like to take a look at our friends south of the border. Many Canadians hesitate to draw comparisons with the United States, but inevitably United States history seems to filter north to become our current events. I thought the remarks of the U. S. Secretary of the Treasury, William Simon, earlier this year were very interesting. He said:
I find three long-term trends disturbing and potentially the most destructive within our economy. The first has been the massive growth of government. .. that has sharply accelerated since the mid-1960's-
A second trend that has been gradually weakening our free enterprise system is... that increases in productive performance are required,... to create new jobs and support a higher standard of living. Yet, as a nation we are rapidly expanding public payments to individuals, but neglecting to provide adequate incentives for new investment-
A third trend that is highly damaging has been the progressive acceleration in the rate of inflation over the past decade.
He concluded:
To attain lasting prosperity, however, we must summon all of the wisdom and strength at our command to attack the more enduring and fundamental forces that grip our economy.
First, we must curb the momentous growth of government in this country ... Second, we must maintain and strengthen the foundations of our free enterprise system by shifting the emphasis of our domestic policies away from consumption and government spending and toward greater savings, investment and capital formation.
The Liberal government of this country does not appear to have reached any of these conclusions. Just before the media reports that Bill C-8 has easily passed the House of Commons, I want to say that I deplore this kind of legislation and that tonight's vote will be my final attempt to save Canadians from further	encroachment by
government.

INDIAN AFFAIRS-WITHDRAWAL OF VOCATIONAL REHABILITATION SERVICES FROM NATIVES IN MANITOBA- REQUEST FOR REVIEW AND REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, early in May I directed a question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) with respect to the withdrawal of the services of the Manitoba vocational rehabilitation branch from treaty Indians in the southwestern part of Manitoba. At that time the minister indicated he did not think this was the fact and gave assurances that these services would be continued to treaty Indians.
I asked a further question on May 27, and by then the minister had become aware of the facts. He defended this withdrawal of services on the basis that it would not do any substantial harm to the problem of chronic unemployability among treaty Indians in this part of Canada.
The operative date for the withdrawal of services was June 30. In the meantime some negotiations had gone on behind the scenes which indicated that the department might change its mind on the matter. It was becoming obvious that to deprive treaty Indians of those services was discriminatory and could even be dealt with by the Human Rights Commission of Manitoba.
The explanation given for the withdrawal was that the responsibility was going to be transferred to the Canada Manpower Centre in the city of Brandon. The centre stated publicly that it did not have the resources to fill the gap in this vital service that would be left on June 30. There is some reference to the Pathfinder Outreach program, which would fill the gap. Unfortunately, the Pathfinder Outreach program is presently in a sad state of disarray, because of internal difficulties.
One of the main projects to be affected is the work activity project in Brandon, which is sponsored by the province of Manitoba and the Government of Canada. Substantial sums of money have been poured into the project, which has been described as one of the most effective to be found in any area of Canada.
The friendship centre at Brandon became concerned and was in touch with departmental officials about the matter. As a result of its intervention, assurance was given in a letter sent by the regional director that, very likely, there would be some revision of thinking and there would not be complete withdrawal of this vitally important service. I have now received a letter from the friendship people indicating that the order went into effect on June 30 and that treaty Indians are no longer being given access to this program.
During the summer months the problem of unemployment appears quiescent, but the crunch will be felt in the fall, with the coming of winter. The chairman of the manpower task force on services to Indian people
Adjournment Debate
expressed the opinion that the arrangement made between the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Manitoba vocational services was the least expensive and most effective way of dealing with the problem of chronic unemployability among treaty Indians.
The fact that this sort of special arrangement serves a useful purpose in particular circumstances was demonstrated when a special arrangement was made in northern Manitoba, where there is a substantial population of treaty Indians out of work. There the Northern Manpower Corps was formed. It was jointly funded by DREE and the province of Manitoba on a 60/40 basis. I suggest that the situation in southwest Manitoba is similar in many respects, and there has to be a special arrangement to meet those particular circumstances. That is why, over the years, very close co-operation was established between the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the provincial vocational services branch.
I trust that either the parliamentary secretary or the minister will assure us this evening that what has been working satisfactorily will not be interfered with and that the atmosphere of confrontation which causes so much damage to our relations with our treaty Indians will not be worsened by any backward step. If the backward step is persisted in, the matter of course would be referred to the Manitoba Human Rights Commission, and we should face a situation of confrontation which does irretrievable damage to good relations between our treaty Indians and the general population.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-WITHDRAWAL OF VOCATIONAL REHABILITATION SERVICES FROM NATIVES IN MANITOBA- REQUEST FOR REVIEW AND REPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answering the hon. member I should like to point out first that there has been no withdrawal of vocational training, counselling and placement services for registered Indians of Manitoba. There is, however, a realignment of resources between the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Manpower and Immigration to produce an effective delivery system for services without duplication of expenditures of federal funds. I am sure that the hon. member, who is interested in the cost effectiveness of government programs, will be happy to hear this.
In essence, as a number of Indian chiefs and band members had expressed some dissatisfaction with the provision of counselling services on their reserves by the Manitoba Vocational Rehabilitation Services, it was agreed in March, 1973, that such services by the Manitoba Vocational Rehabilitation Services would be restricted to status Indian people in urban areas and that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development would provide such services to those Indians living on reserves. These changes were introduced on a gradually phased basis in order not to disrupt any existing services.
As the situation now stands, the Department of Manpower and Immigration is officially responsible for employment-related services to all Canadians. Moreover those status Indians who have fulfilled the urban residency requirements are also entitled to services of the Manitoba Vocational Rehabilitation Service in the same manner as any other urban residents of Manitoba. Arrangements have also been made that counsellors of Indian Affairs would assist any status Indians who do not
7478

July 10, 1975
Adjournment Debate
meet the residency qualifications of Manitoba for service, upon referral by the Manitoba Vocational Rehabilitation Service.
With respect to the services being provided by the Department of Manpower and Immigration, officials of both departments finalized administrative details to add four to five additional out-reach workers to the staff of the Manitoba region of the Department of Manpower. Status Indian trainees already enrolled in the Manitoba Vocational Rehabilitation Services' programs will continue until graduation at the expense of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
Taking all factors into consideration, there is confidence that the new arrangement will be more effective and acceptable to all of the Indian people served, both urban and non-urban, and at the same time will be more economical by avoiding duplication of services.

subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-PROPOSED LAY-OFF OF THREE THOUSAND MAINTENANCE WORKERS-REQUEST FOR REPORT
CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-PROPOSED LAY-OFF OF THREE THOUSAND MAINTENANCE WORKERS-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 2 I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) whether he had had an opportunity to look into the announcement by CPR that it would lay off 3,000 workers, 1,200 in Montreal and over 1,000 in Winnipeg, until the end of September. The minister replied that he had made inquiries with the CNR which was making virtually no lay-offs, and that the CPR lay-offs were a matter of negotiation with the union.
I asked the minister in charge of the wheat board a supplementary question. I asked whether he would look into the question of whether, as a result of this lay-off, there would be a shortage of freight cars to move grain this fall, and whether he would look into the question of whether the lay-off was in fact pressure being put on the workers by CPR ahead of their forthcoming contract negotiations this fall. The minister thought this was pretty far-fetched, but promised to look into the question of the possible shortfall of freight cars.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) have recently spoken quite frequently about |he difficulties created in various segments of the Canadian economy as a result of one small group of workers belonging to one union, in a field in which there are many unions, going on strike and tying up the whole industry.
In the railway industry there are 18 unions which represent all the employees. For a number of years they have banded together and bargained. One agreement is reached with the CPR and CNR. However, we now have a situation where the CPR has unilaterally decided on a major lay off of workers in the shop craft industry, particularly the carmen. We have 3,000 workers, many of them with ten or 20 years' seniority, who have worked continuously for the CPR, being given a seven weeks holiday without pay.
I suggest this is not at all far-fetched. I suggest, as I did in my question the other day, that the CPR is beginning the process of negotiating with its employees by warning

them that they better not ask for too much in the negotiations this October because their jobs are not that secure.
The CPR is supposedly worrying about the cash flow of the company. However, at its recent annual general meeting of shareholders, the chairman of CPR, Mr. Ian D. Sinclair, announced record profits in 1974 of $185.5 million, 50 per cent higher than those for 1973, and double the take of 1972. It is true that more than half of the profits came from the conglomerates owned and controlled by CP, but these are essentially in the natural resource field and arise from concessions given to the CP when the original promoters were encouraged to build the railway.
In recent years there have been a number of serious accidents as a result of derailments. The Canadian Transport Commission investigated the situation, held hearings, and recommended that maintenance work be increased sharply; it concluded that the derailments were a result of the lack of maintenance work on the rails.
We are expecting a plentiful crop this fall in western Canada, and again we are faced with the fact that once more Canada is likely to be unable to meet its commitments for grain sales since. According to the railway companies there will be a shortage of freight cars to move the grain. I suggest that this is a time not to be laying off railroad workers but to be putting them to work repairing and reconditioning all the old freight cars which can be made available for use, so that the big crop we are expecting this fall may be moved expeditiously both to the Lakehead and to Vancouver to meet the demands of customers.
I would urge the ministers concerned to use their influence with Canadian Pacific-and it is considerable-to urge that the company rescind these lay-offs which have been announced, that it put the workers to work doing the work they are ready to do and which is so necessary for the well being of the country.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Iona Campagnolo (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY-PROPOSED LAY-OFF OF THREE THOUSAND MAINTENANCE WORKERS-REQUEST FOR REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) with respect to the part of the question which concerns the Department of Transport, may I say he has described the situation in which the Canadian Pacific finds itself, that of having to lay off a large number of workers for an extended period over the summer due to a general decline in the economy.
As the hon. member knows, the Canadian Pacific is a privately owned company, and in matters affecting its labour relations the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) exercises no jurisdiction. He has, however, been assured by CP Rail that there should be no problems in supplying cars for the 1975-76 grain shipping season. There is surplus equipment on CP Rail, including covered hoppers, due to a fall-off in potash loadings; partners in split-lease arrangements are asking CP Rail to keep cars year-round until the economy picks up. In addition, some grain boxes are being stored due to a fall-off of grain shipments. At the present time CP Rail has more than a thousand government covered hoppers, with over 2,000 more coming on-stream in January.
The suggestion by the hon. member that involved in these lay-offs is a ploy by CP Rail to put pressure on the
July 10, 1975

government to raise the rate paid for the movement of grain is clearly unfounded.
As regards Canadian National Railways, this company does not intend to lay off maintenance workers in large numbers as CP Rail has been forced to do. CN lay-offs are not expected to exceed very small numbers as required in the normal course of events to adjust the work force to local needs. As a result, grain shipments will not be adversely affected in any way.

subtopic: FOOD PRICES REVIEW BOARD-REPORT ON FISH PRICES- POSSIBILITY OF REFERENCE TO COMBINES INVESTIGATION BRANCH
FOOD PRICES REVIEW BOARD-REPORT ON FISH PRICES- POSSIBILITY OF REFERENCE TO COMBINES INVESTIGATION BRANCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) has remained behind to hear what I have to say. I am pleased to have this opportunity to follow up my question of June 27 to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), which, stated very simply, was this. I asked whether, in vew of the fact that the Food Prices Review Board report on fisheries indicated a wide discrepancy between the wholesale and retail prices of fish, from 49 cents a pound to $1.08 a pound, the minister intended to bring the matter to the attention of the combines investigation branch of his department. The minister replied that as a result of the excellent report of the Food Prices Review Board he hoped that he would be able to take action on the recommendations. Further, on requesting action on anti-profiteering legislation, the minister indicated appropriate action would be taken.
Naturally the discrepancy that I mentioned between wholesale and retail prices is further aggravated when one considers the spread between the price paid to the fishermen and the price paid by the consumer, which is more frightening. The spread in price in some cases reaches some 1,000 to 2,000 per cent, if one can imagine such a spread.
While I recognize that the yield of some delicate species of fish justifies a variance, it is a wonder that Canadian consumers do pay, for example, approximately $1.50 for a couple of ounces of herring processed outside Canada, which originally brought the fishermen 31/2 cents a pound in Canada at the wharf. This suggests to me that something is wrong or fishy, and is an indication of the inefficiency of our government's marketing policy regarding our fish resources.
Not only is there inefficiency, Mr. Speaker, but complacency, apathy, and a complete disregard for the value of our fish stocks as a source of protein and nutrition not only for the poor of Canada but, internationally, for the poor and poverty stricken of the world. Furthermore, the department shows a blatant disregard for its responsibility.
Almost each and every day in this House of Commons we hear references to prices of food and the difficulties experienced by the people of Canada. Indeed, there is reference to the ineptitude of government in controlling the price of beef, pork, poultry, eggs, and other commodities which we have in abundance in Canada. For some reason or other we ignore the renewable resources of the sea which, if protected by our government, could provide a
Adjournment Debate
protein-rich food resource at a reasonable price to the consumer, in spite of inflationary pressures, on a continuing basis.
I have made reference to the herring species, but there are many other examples of fish the price of which indicate rip-off profits, such as cod, mackerel, lobster, salmon, halibut and many other species available in Canada.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has the ammunition to investigate this atrocious practice, and I wonder what he is waiting for before implementing legislation that would prevent this rip-off of many people in Canada. The government is always asking members of the opposition for suggestions. In many cases I have tried to co-operate. In this case I can only ask the minister to investigate the system of pricing from the fishermen through to the buyer, the processing plant, or even beyond, to determine the discrepancy which exists. This would render invaluable service to the Canadian consumer.

speakeroldname: Mr. Norman A. Cafik (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: FOOD PRICES REVIEW BOARD-REPORT ON FISH PRICES- POSSIBILITY OF REFERENCE TO COMBINES INVESTIGATION BRANCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) has raised an important question. In his remarks tonight I think he has gone beyond the specific question of the pricing of fish to the whole question of the fisheries and its importance in terms of protein, nutrients, etc.
If I may deal with the specific question as it relates to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, I should first of all say that, as the hon. member knows, the Food Prices Review Board has conducted an investigation which was confined primarily to the Toronto area. We have taken a great deal of interest in its findings and we hope it will pursue the whole question to find out whether, from its point of view, these spreads are justified.
I should point out to the hon. members of this House that we in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs do not have the legislative base to set some kind of prices or margins on prices. As the hon. member knows, prior to the 1974 election we introduced a bill, called the anti-profiteering bill, which would have given us the legislative authority to take action in connection with what the hon. member might call rip-off prices. That bill was not passed due to the opposition of his own party and other opposition parties in this House, so we are without that legislative base from which to take action.
Subsequently we indicated that it is our intention in the department to bring forward an anti-profiteering bill which would again give us some legislative base to deal with that kind of question on a selective basis. I think it is a very important thing, and we do need this legislative base. When we have the authority from parliament, action of that type may well be taken on these important occasions.
To suggest that we do have the legislative authority to taken action in terms of investigation is true under the Combines Investigation Act, through the director of investigation and research. However, I think the hon. member and all Canadians ought to know that in the action we can take there is no relationship to the setting of prices, but only relationship to collusion or the fixing of prices between differing groups within the market place. We see no
7480

July 10, 1975
Adjournment Debate
evidence that this in fact is occurring at the moment. If the hon. member, or any other Canadian feels there is some evidence that would warrant an investigation by the director under the Combines Investigation Act in relation to collusion or price fixing we would be the first ones who would want to know about it and to take action under the legislation which now exists.
